summary: This standards-track document extends PA-TNC (RFC 5792) with attributes and message exchanges that let endpoints report their installed software inventory to a NEA Server. It is part of the Network Endpoint Assessment work.

eli5.summary: A computer tells the security helper what programs it has installed, like handing over a list of toys.

questions: how do endpoints report installed software inventory
what is an eid epoch in swima
subtitle: How an endpoint tells a network server which software is installed, and keeps that list up to date as it changes.

tldr.problem: Knowing which software is installed on endpoints helps enforce policy and find exposure to attack, but there was no standard way for an endpoint to report it to a NEA Server.
tldr.mechanism: SWIMA defines PA-TNC attributes. A Posture Validator sends a request, and the endpoint's Posture Collector answers with an inventory or a list of change events, either once or continuously through a subscription. Events carry sequential identifiers within an epoch so the server can keep a remote copy in sync.
tldr.outcome: SWIMA standardizes the transport only, not how software is detected, and the RFC says the reported data cannot be treated as completely accurate. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8412 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reporting Installed Software
sections.content:
A list of the software on endpoints helps a network operator understand and maintain its security state. If policy requires some software and prohibits other software, an inventory can show compliance. An inventory can also be compared with vulnerability or threat alerts to judge an endpoint's exposure to attack.

SWIMA (Software Inventory Message and Attributes) is a standard way to exchange this data. It extends PA-TNC (RFC 5792) and moves software identification, installation and characterization information from an endpoint to a central server. It does not standardize how software is detected. Instead it relies on "data sources" such as ISO SWID tag files, third-party inventory tools and package managers.

The scope is deliberate. SWIMA reports only software that is installed. It does not report what is running, and it does not report individual files, libraries or installation packages. The RFC notes the mechanisms could also carry firmware and operating system information. Part of the motivation was the IETF's Security Automation and Continuous Monitoring (SACM) architecture, but SWIMA has no dependency on it.
sections.eli5: It is a standard way for a computer to hand over a list of the programs installed on it, so a helper can check whether they are safe and allowed.

sections.title: Players: SWIMA-PC and SWIMA-PV
sections.content:
SWIMA lives inside the Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) architecture (RFC 5209). On the endpoint, a Posture Collector gathers information. On the NEA Server, a Posture Validator receives it. They talk over the PA-TNC interface, carried in PB-TNC (RFC 5793) messages, which in turn run over a transport such as PT-TLS (RFC 6876) or PT-EAP (RFC 7171).

  • A SWIMA-PC is a Posture Collector that conforms to this specification. It receives requests and sends responses.
  • A SWIMA-PV is a Posture Validator that conforms to this specification. It sends requests and processes responses.

The records come from the endpoint's Software Inventory Evidence Collection. Each Software Inventory Evidence Record corresponds to one installed instance of a software product as reported by one data source. The RFC assumes the broker layers provide reliable delivery, meaning a message is delivered or the sender learns it failed. Without that, features such as subscriptions might not behave as expected.
sections.eli5: One helper lives on the computer and keeps the list. Another helper lives on the server and asks for it. The two talk through a set of agreed messages.

sections.title: Sources, Identifiers and Records
sections.content:
Records come from one or more sources, and no single source is expected to be perfect. A SWIMA-PC does not have to use every source, but for each source it does use it MUST fully support the specification, and it MUST include the data from all its supported sources every time it reports. Otherwise a server could wrongly conclude that software was removed. Duplicates are allowed: if two sources report the same installation, both records are kept.

Every reported record carries a common set of fields:

  • Software Identifier: a string for a specific version of a specific software product, derived by rules of the record's data model. SWIMA treats it as opaque. It is a fraction of the size of the full record, so it is often more efficient to collect inventories by identifier and fetch full records only when needed.
  • Data Model Type: a PEN plus a type number saying how the record is structured. PEN 0 is reserved by IANA, and type values from 0xC0 (192) up are for local enterprise use.
  • Record Identifier: a 4-byte unsigned integer assigned by the SWIMA-PC to each record, which lets a server tell apart several installs of the same product.
  • Software Locator: a URI saying where the software is installed, normally with the file scheme. If the location cannot be determined it is zero-length.
  • Source Identifier: an 8-bit unsigned integer naming the source, with no reserved values and at most 256 sources. It helps recognize a source rather than identify it.

SWIMA does not constrain the data model. The SWIMA-PV treats record bodies as black boxes and MUST NOT reject a message because of the data model. The SWIMA-PC must be able to generate Software Identifiers for the data models in section 6, which are ISO 2015 and ISO 2009 SWID tags using XML.
sections.eli5: Each toy on the list gets a name tag (what it is), a number (which copy it is), a place (where it sits) and a note about who told us about it.

sections.title: Attributes and Messages
sections.content:
SWIMA attributes use the PA-TNC format and travel in PB-TNC messages that carry the new SWIMA Attributes PA Subtype. All attributes have a vendor PEN of 0x000000. Numeric values are sent in network (big endian) byte order, and text fields are normalized to Network Unicode (RFC 5198) where the RFC says so.

The SWIMA Request is the only request for inventory data. Its flags say whether to clear this PV's subscriptions, whether to subscribe, and whether the response should include evidence records (Result Type). It also holds a Software Identifier Count, a Request ID, and an Earliest EID. If the Earliest EID is zero the PV wants an inventory. If it is non-zero the PV wants events starting at that EID. A non-zero Software Identifier Count makes the request targeted.

Together the Result Type flag and the Earliest EID pick exactly one response type: Software Identifier Inventory, Software Identifier Events, Software Inventory or Software Events. The two attributes with identifiers only (no full records) can be smaller by multiple orders of magnitude. Event records hold an EID, a timestamp, a record identifier, data model type, source, an action and the identifier and locator. The action is 1 for CREATION, 2 for DELETION or 3 for ALTERATION. Timestamps are 20-octet RFC 3339 strings in UTC.

Two further pairs of attributes cover status. A Subscription Status Request and Response list the PV's active subscriptions, and a Source Metadata Request and Response describe the PC's data sources. A SWIMA-PC MUST support both status exchanges, and PVs are recommended to.
sections.eli5: There is one kind of question, "what do you have, or what changed?", and a few kinds of answer, from a short list of names to a long list with all the details.

sections.title: Events, EIDs and Epochs
sections.content:
The software on an endpoint changes. A SWIMA-PC MUST detect the creation, deletion and alteration of records in close to real time (within seconds) while running. If it was not running, it MUST work out the net change over that period. It MUST also give each change a time, and for deletions it MUST keep a copy of the deleted record for a reasonable time. A record change must keep the same Software Identifier, so applying a patch that changes the version is a deletion followed by a creation, not an alteration.

Changes are ordered by an Event Identifier (EID), a 4-byte unsigned integer assigned sequentially, in the context of an EID Epoch, also a 4-byte unsigned integer. EID 0 is reserved: in a request it means "send an inventory", and in a response it means the state before any events, so the first event in an epoch is 1. There must be no coverage gaps in the event records. If the PC cannot guarantee that, for example after a crash that loses its place, it MUST pick a new EID Epoch, chosen to avoid reuse, and purge older events.

Every response carries the EID Epoch and the Last EID. A PV can store an inventory together with the EID it reflects, then later ask only for events from the next EID. A change of epoch tells the PV there is a discontinuity, and only a full inventory can bring it back in sync. If the PV sees gaps within an epoch it can re-request events or fetch a full inventory.

If a list of events would be too large (the PA-TNC attribute limit is 4 GB, or the PC may have a smaller limit), the PC MAY return a partial list and include a Last Consulted EID. When the Last Consulted EID is less than the Last EID the PV asks again starting from one more than the Last Consulted EID. There is no way to return a partial inventory.
sections.eli5: Imagine a diary where every change gets a page number. If you know the last page you read, you only need the pages after it. If the diary is swapped for a new one, you must read it from the start.

sections.title: Subscriptions
sections.content:
Instead of asking each time, a SWIMA-PV can set the Subscribe flag in a SWIMA Request. The PC replies directly as usual, and then pushes a response whenever a relevant change occurs. All SWIMA-PCs and SWIMA-PVs MUST support subscriptions. The subscription's ID is the Request ID of the establishing request. A PC MUST support at least 8 simultaneous subscriptions and a PV at least 256. A PC that cannot take another answers with a SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_DENIED_ERROR.

What gets pushed copies the establishing request. An inventory subscription sends the whole inventory after each relevant change, and an event subscription sends only the new events, with no event reported twice. A targeted subscription sends only data about the named Software Identifiers. A PC MUST NOT merge the data for several subscriptions, but it MAY delay a push briefly to bundle events for one subscription, as long as every event is still reported and the delay can be disabled.

A PV ends its subscriptions by setting the Clear Subscriptions flag, which clears all of them for that PB-TNC connection and Posture Validator Identifier, not individual ones. A PC cannot end a subscription on its own, except that a fulfilment error or a closed connection cancels it.
sections.eli5: It is like asking a friend to text you every time the list changes, instead of asking again and again.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
Errors use the PA-TNC Error attribute with SWIMA-specific codes. The behavior is all or nothing: a PC that finds an error in a request MUST NOT act on any part of it, and it sends an error instead of a response, never both. A SWIMA-PV MUST NOT send PA-TNC Errors to a PC. It should log the problem instead. Both sides SHOULD log errors.

The codes the RFC defines for SWIMA are:

  • SWIMA_ERROR (4): a fatal error specific to SWIMA processing that fits no other code.
  • SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_DENIED_ERROR (5): the PC refused to establish or clear subscriptions.
  • SWIMA_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE_ERROR (6): the response was too large, and the error says the largest size the PC supports.
  • SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_FULFILLMENT_ERROR (7): an error while fulfilling a subscription, which cancels that subscription for both sides.
  • SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_ID_REUSE_ERROR (8): a request reused the ID of an active subscription, which does not cancel the subscription.
sections.eli5: If a request is wrong, the helper does none of it and says what went wrong, so nothing gets half done.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC is frank that inventory data is imperfect: tools may update late, may mischaracterize software, and some software may not be tracked at all. Users of SWIMA data cannot treat it as completely accurate, though it can still show useful problems. SWIMA does not try to detect an endpoint that reports false information.

The data is also sensitive. An inventory can reveal versions, patch levels, install locations, supply chain details and, through timestamps, how quickly an organization applies patches. Central inventories should be protected against unauthorized access. SWIMA has no confidentiality mechanism of its own, so implementers must use suitable NEA transports. The PC MUST protect the integrity of its event records and subscription records, and it should have no more permissions than it needs. Content from sources must be sanitized, because anyone might create a file that becomes a record.

On privacy, an inventory can allow inferences about a user, such as hobbies or the financial institutions they use. Organizations should make sure users know about the collection and limit access to people trained in privacy requirements.
sections.eli5: A list of everything on your computer tells a lot about you, so it has to be kept safe and the list is never perfect.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Clear Subscriptions, Subscribe and Result Type flags; the other bits are reserved.

fields.name: Software Identifier Count
fields.desc: Non-zero means a targeted request; sub-blocks follow.

fields.name: Request ID
fields.desc: Identifies the request; becomes the Subscription ID if one is set up.

fields.name: Earliest EID
fields.desc: Zero requests an inventory; non-zero requests events from that EID.

items.label: SWIMA Request
items.desc: PV asks the PC for an inventory or events; may set up a subscription.

items.label: Subscription Status Request
items.desc: Asks for the PV's active subscriptions.

items.label: Source Metadata Request
items.desc: Asks about the PC's data sources.

messages.label: SWIMA Response
messages.note: Direct response to the establishing request.

messages.label: SWIMA Response
messages.note: Sent after a change event, in fulfillment of the subscription.

messages.label: SWIMA Response
messages.note: Sent after the next change event.

items.label: SWIMA_ERROR
items.desc: Fatal SWIMA-specific error not covered below.

items.label: SWIMA_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE_ERROR
items.desc: Response too large to be serviced.

items.label: SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_FULFILLMENT_ERROR
items.desc: Error while fulfilling a subscription; it is cancelled.

items.label: SWIMA_SUBSCRIPTION_ID_REUSE_ERROR
items.desc: Request ID matches an active Subscription ID.
